references.title: ACCA: performance appraisal and working-capital ratios

formula.name: Debt-to-equity
formula.expression: Total debt / total equity
inputs: Total debt: borrowings under the declared debt definition.
Total equity: equity on the matching consolidated/entity basis.
formula.scope: Use the same period, currency, accounting perimeter and definition for compared inputs. A zero denominator is undefined; negative bases can change or defeat the usual interpretation. Higher/lower is not an automatic quality score.
original: Debt-to-Equity Ratio = Total Debt / Total Equity
Amount of debt a company has in relation to its equity. The lower the ratio, the less the debt compared to its equity.

formula.name: Debt-to-assets
formula.expression: Total debt / total assets
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Total debt: the chosen borrowing measure, not automatically all liabilities.
Total assets: recognized assets at the matching reporting date.
formula.scope: Use the same period, currency, accounting perimeter and definition for compared inputs. A zero denominator is undefined; negative bases can change or defeat the usual interpretation. Higher/lower is not an automatic quality score.
original: Debt-to-Assets Ratio = Total Debt / Total Asset
Amount of debt a company has in relation to its assets. The lower the ration, the less the debt compared to assets.

formula.name: Current ratio
formula.expression: Current assets / current liabilities
inputs: Current assets: assets classified as current.
Current liabilities: obligations classified as current.
formula.scope: Classification and realizability matter; compare like business models and dates. Use the same period, currency, accounting perimeter and definition for compared inputs. A zero denominator is undefined; negative bases can change or defeat the usual interpretation. Higher/lower is not an automatic quality score.
original: Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities
Measures whether a company has enough short-term assets to cover its short-term liabilities. The higher the ratio, the more assets you have in relation to your liabilities.

formula.name: Equity multiplier
formula.expression: Total assets / total equity
inputs: Total assets: recognized asset base.
Total equity: equity on the same entity and date basis.
formula.scope: Non-equity funding includes liabilities beyond interest-bearing debt. For DuPont, use compatible averages.
original: Equity Multiplier = Total Assets / Total Equity

Measures the proportion of a company's assets that are financed through debt versus equity. A high equity multiplier means the company is relying more on debt to finance it's assets rather than equity.

formula.name: Quick ratio
formula.expression: (Current assets − inventory − prepayments − other non-quick current assets) / current liabilities
inputs: Quick assets: cash, eligible liquid investments and collectible receivables under the stated definition.
Current liabilities: matching short-term obligations.
formula.scope: The source’s assets-minus-inventory shortcut assumes the remaining assets are quick. State exclusions and receivable quality.
original: Quick Ratio = (Current Assets - Inventory) / Current Liabilities
Shows the ability of a company to meet its short-term obligations with its most liquid assets. The high the ratio, the more liquidity your business has.

formula.name: Cash ratio
formula.expression: Cash and cash equivalents / current liabilities
inputs: Cash and equivalents: eligible cash balances and cash equivalents.
Current liabilities: matching short-term obligations.
formula.scope: State restrictions on cash and any different convention for liquid investments. Use the same period, currency, accounting perimeter and definition for compared inputs. A zero denominator is undefined; negative bases can change or defeat the usual interpretation. Higher/lower is not an automatic quality score.
original: Cash Ratio = Cash and Cash Equivalent / Current Liabilities
Amount of cash and equivalents a company has in relation to its current liabilities. The higher the ratio, the more cash you have in comparison with your current liabilities.

formula.name: Net working capital
formula.expression: Current assets − current liabilities
inputs: Current assets: current balance-sheet assets.
Current liabilities: current balance-sheet obligations.
formula.scope: This broad balance-sheet measure differs from noncash operating working capital used in valuation. Negative working capital is not automatically distress.
original: Net Working capital = Current Assets - Current Liabilities
Short-term liquidity and its ability to meet its current obligations. Higher NWC indicates that the company has a comfortable cushion of liquid assets to cover its short-term liabilities.

formula.name: Net working capital to total assets
formula.expression: (Current assets − current liabilities) / total assets
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Net working capital: current assets less current liabilities.
Total assets: the matching recognized asset base.
formula.scope: This measures working capital relative to total assets, not the current ratio.
original: Net Working Capital Ratio = (Current Assets - Current Liabilities) / Total Assets
Showcases the difference between a company's current asset and its current liabilities. The higher the ratio, the more current assets you have compared to your current liabilities.

formula.name: Debt-to-capitalisation
formula.expression: Debt / (debt + equity)
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Debt: borrowings under the declared convention.
Equity: a compatible book or market equity value.
formula.scope: Do not mix book debt and market equity without stating the purpose and convention. Use the same period, currency, accounting perimeter and definition for compared inputs. A zero denominator is undefined; negative bases can change or defeat the usual interpretation. Higher/lower is not an automatic quality score.
original: Total Debt-to-Capitalisation Ratio = Total Debt / (Total Debt + Shareholders' Equity)
The total amount of debt in relation to a company's total capitalisation (debt & equity). The lower ratio, the less your business is captailised using debt.

formula.name: Liabilities to adjusted tangible net worth
formula.expression: Total liabilities / (equity − intangibles − prepayments − related-party receivables)
inputs: Total liabilities: the declared obligation base.
Adjusted tangible net worth: equity after the listed deductions.
formula.scope: This is the source’s lender-style adjustment, not a universal net-worth definition. Contract definitions and a positive denominator are essential.
original: Tangible Net Worth Ratio = Total Liabilities / (Total Equity - Intangible Assets - Prepaid Assets - Due from Related Parties)
The value of all your assets and the size of all your liabilities

sections.heading: Bank capital adequacy: a specialist measure

formula.name: Bank total-capital adequacy
formula.expression: (Eligible Tier 1 capital + eligible Tier 2 capital) / risk-weighted assets × 100
inputs: Eligible regulatory capital: capital recognized under the applicable regime.
Risk-weighted assets: the regime’s risk-weighted denominator.
formula.scope: This is regulatory capital coverage, not cash liquidity. No current threshold, buffer or compliance conclusion is supplied.
original: Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) = (Tier 1 Capital + Tier 2 Capital) / (Risk-Weighted Assets) x 100
Not liquid assets but bookkeeping of assets and liability

title: Returns and asset efficiency: earnings, sales and capital
summary: Interpret returns on assets/equity and turnover of assets, receivables, payables and stock.
takeaway: Use consistent sales, cost and balance definitions; averages and closing balances are not interchangeable.
notes: The source’s total-asset-turnover expression uses subtraction. The reviewed measure divides net sales by average total assets. Fixed-asset turnover may use average net fixed assets; the source uses a point-in-time denominator.

references.title: ACCA: performance appraisal and working-capital ratios

formula.name: Return on assets
formula.expression: Net income / average total assets
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Net income: attributable earnings for the selected entity/period.
Average assets: preferably time-weighted assets; opening/closing mean is a shortcut.
formula.scope: Use the same period, currency, accounting perimeter and definition for compared inputs. A zero denominator is undefined; negative bases can change or defeat the usual interpretation. Higher/lower is not an automatic quality score.
original: Return on Assets (RoA) = Net Income / Average Total Assets
Amount of net income a company generates in relation to its total assets. The higher your RoA, the better your return on your assets.

formula.name: Return on equity
formula.expression: Attributable net income / average corresponding equity
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Attributable income: earnings matching the equity owners being measured.
Average corresponding equity: compatible average owner capital.
formula.scope: Match common versus total-shareholder earnings and equity. Use the same period, currency, accounting perimeter and definition for compared inputs. A zero denominator is undefined; negative bases can change or defeat the usual interpretation. Higher/lower is not an automatic quality score.
original: Return on Equity (RoE) = Net Income / Average Shareholders' Equity
Amount of net income a company generates in relation to its equity. The higher your RoE, the better return you are getting on your equity.

formula.name: Total asset turnover
formula.expression: Net sales / average total assets
inputs: Net sales: period sales after relevant returns/allowances.
Average total assets: assets used over the same period.
formula.scope: The source subtracts assets from sales. Turnover divides period sales by the asset base.
original: Total Asset Turnover = Net Sales - Average Total Assets
A company generates for each dollar of total assets it holds. Higher TAT suggests that the company is generating more sales relative to its investment in assets.

formula.name: Receivables turnover
formula.expression: Net credit sales / average trade receivables
inputs: Net credit sales: sales creating the receivables being measured.
Average trade receivables: matching collectible customer balance.
formula.scope: Use compatible sales tax, credit/cash sales and receivable definitions.
original: Accounts Receivables Turnover = Net Credit Sales / Average Accounts Receivable
Measures how quickly a company collects outstanding debts from customers

formula.name: Payables turnover
formula.expression: Credit purchases / average trade payables
inputs: Credit purchases: purchases creating the supplier liability.
Average trade payables: matching supplier balance.
formula.scope: The source says total supplier purchases. Cost of sales is only a disclosed proxy when appropriate.
original: Accounts Payable Turnover = Total Supplier Purchases / Average Accounts Payable
Measures how quickly a company pays its suppliers

formula.name: Inventory turnover
formula.expression: Cost of goods sold / average inventory
inputs: COGS: cost of the stock sold over the period.
Average inventory: matching stock on a consistent valuation basis.
formula.scope: Use the same period, currency, accounting perimeter and definition for compared inputs. A zero denominator is undefined; negative bases can change or defeat the usual interpretation. Higher/lower is not an automatic quality score.
original: Inventory Turnover = CoGS / Average Inventory
Meassures the number of times inventory is sold and replaced during a period

formula.name: Fixed-asset turnover
formula.expression: Revenue / average net fixed assets
inputs: Revenue: compatible period sales.
Average net fixed assets: carrying values of productive fixed assets over the period.
formula.scope: The source uses net fixed assets without averaging. A closing-base convention must be disclosed; asset age and leasing affect comparisons.
original: Fixed Asset Turnover = Revenue / Net Fixed Assets
Measures how effectively a company uses its fixed assets to generate sales

title: Margins, returns and the DuPont bridge
summary: Distinguish profit margins, investment returns, dividend measures and the drivers of return on equity.
takeaway: A margin, a return on invested money and a dividend payout ratio have different denominators.
steps: DuPont: separate the actual identity from a list of ratios
notes: The source’s DuPont line lists families of ratios; multiplying all of them is not a valid identity. The reviewed three-factor bridge uses net margin, total-asset turnover and the equity multiplier on consistent bases.

formula.name: Gross profit margin
formula.expression: Gross profit / matching net sales
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Gross profit: matching revenue less cost of sales.
Net sales: revenue on the same basis.
formula.scope: Use the same period, currency, accounting perimeter and definition for compared inputs. A zero denominator is undefined; negative bases can change or defeat the usual interpretation. Higher/lower is not an automatic quality score.
original: Gross Profit Margin = Gross Profit / Net Sales
% of revenue that exceeds the CoGS.

formula.name: Accounting return on investment
formula.expression: Defined period net profit / defined investment base
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Net profit: profit attributed to the investment.
Investment base: stated initial or average investment convention.
formula.scope: The source’s accounting ratio differs from total investment holding-period return and needs a time horizon.
original: Return on Investment (RoI) = Net Profit / Total Investment
The return on investment capital invested in a business.

formula.name: Return on capital employed
formula.expression: Compatible operating profit / stated capital employed
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Operating profit: period earnings on the chosen basis.
Capital employed: stated operating-capital definition and average/closing timing.
formula.scope: Assets less current liabilities and long-term debt plus equity are common starting bases; adjustments and timing must be consistent.
original: Return on Capital Employed (RoCE) = Operating Profit / Capital Employed
A company's ability to generate profits from the capital its has invested in its business.

formula.name: Basic earnings per common share
formula.expression: (Attributable net income − applicable preferred dividends) / weighted-average common shares
inputs: Attributable income: earnings matching common owners.
Preferred dividends: applicable preference deduction.
Weighted shares: period common share count.
formula.scope: This simplified basic-EPS bridge is not a diluted-EPS or full participation-rights model.
original: Earnings Per Share (EPS) = (Net Income - Preferred Dividends) / Weighted Average Shares Outstanding
The portion of a company's profit allocated to each outstanding share of common stock.

formula.name: Operating profit margin
formula.expression: Operating profit / matching revenue
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Operating profit: declared operating subtotal.
Revenue: matching period revenue.
formula.scope: Use the same period, currency, accounting perimeter and definition for compared inputs. A zero denominator is undefined; negative bases can change or defeat the usual interpretation. Higher/lower is not an automatic quality score.
original: Operating Profit Margin = Operating Profit / Revenue
% of revenue that remains after deducting operating expenses.

formula.name: Dividend yield
formula.expression: Annual dividend per corresponding share / market price per share
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Annual dividend: stated historical/forward convention.
Market price: corresponding class and date.
formula.scope: Not a total return or guaranteed future payout; disclose special-dividend treatment.
original: Dividend Yield = Annual Dividend per Share / Market Price per Share
Return on investment from dividends

formula.name: Gross margin: revenue-cost form
formula.expression: (Revenue − corresponding cost of sales) / revenue
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Revenue/cost of sales: same period and activity scope.
formula.scope: Equivalent to gross profit/revenue when the underlying definitions match.
original: Gross Margin Ratio = (Revenue - CoGS) / Revenue
Measures the profitablity of a company's products or services

sections.heading: DuPont: separate the actual identity from a list of ratios

formula.name: Three-factor DuPont identity
formula.expression: ROE = (net income / net sales) × (net sales / average total assets) × (average total assets / average equity)
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Net income/sales: matching period measures.
Average assets/equity: compatible averages and owners.
formula.scope: The source lists many related ratios rather than an algebraic identity. Do not multiply every item in that list.
original: Dupont Analysis = Net Profit Margin, Profitability (Gross Profit Margin, Operating Profit Margin, Pre-tax Profit Margin, Effective Tax Rate) x Asset Turnover, Efficiency (Fixed Asset Turnover, AR Turnover, AP Turnover, Inventory Turnover) x Financial Leverage (Debt Ratio, Equity Ratio)

items: To decompose the different drivers of return on equity

formula.name: Dividend payout ratio
formula.expression: Corresponding dividends / corresponding earnings
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Dividends/earnings: matched common or total-owner basis and period.
formula.scope: Losses, preference distributions and one-off dividends can make simple comparisons misleading.
original: Dividend Payout Ratio = Dividends / net income

items: The proportion of earnings paid out as dividends to shareholders.

title: Debt coverage: earnings measures and covenant definitions
summary: Compare EBITDA-based coverage and leverage while distinguishing contractual tests from universal ratios.
takeaway: A covenant is governed by its agreement’s definitions, adjustments and testing dates.
steps: Coverage, fixed charges and funded-debt leverage
notes: EBIT/interest and EBITDA/interest are different conventions. Debt-service coverage may use cash available for debt service rather than EBITDA. The fixed-charge expression cannot be verified as a universal covenant without the actual agreement.

sections.heading: Coverage, fixed charges and funded-debt leverage

formula.name: EBITDA-based interest coverage
formula.expression: EBITDA / compatible interest expense
inputs: EBITDA: declared earnings measure.
Interest expense: matching test period and definition.
formula.scope: Different from EBIT/interest and cash-interest coverage. A covenant may define each input differently.
original: Interest Coverage = EBITDA / Interest Expense

blocks.text: Ability to generate enough operating income to cover its interest obligations. Higher ICR indicates that the company's operating income is sufficiently higher than its interest expenses.

formula.name: EBITDA-based debt-service proxy
formula.expression: EBITDA / (scheduled principal + compatible interest)
inputs: EBITDA: chosen period earnings measure.
Debt service: matching scheduled principal and interest.
formula.scope: This proxy does not fund taxes, investment or working capital. It is not a universal cash DSCR or agreement test.
original: Debt Service Coverage = EBITDA / (Principal + Interest)

blocks.text: Ability to meet its debt obligations. Higher (DSC) indicates that the company's operating income is more than sufficient to meet its debt obligations.

formula.name: Fixed-charge coverage: agreement-specific
inputs: Fixed charges, cash taxes, unfunded CAPEX, distributions and P/I: terms requiring their agreement definitions.
formula.scope: The source expression cannot be certified as a universal covenant without the agreement, test period and adjustment rules. Original wording is retained for review.
original: Fixed Charged Coverage = (EBITDA + Fixed Charges - Cash Taxes - Unfunded CAPEX - Shareholder Distribution) / (P + I + Fixed Charges)

blocks.text: Ability to meet its fixed financial obligations. Higher FCC indicates that the company's operating income is sufficient to cover both its fixed financial obligations and interest expenses.

formula.name: Funded debt to EBITDA
formula.expression: Defined funded debt / compatible EBITDA
inputs: Funded debt: debt included by the chosen convention/agreement.
EBITDA: compatible period earnings.
formula.scope: State leases, guarantees, adjustments, trailing-period basis and negative-EBITDA limitations.
original: Funded Debt to EBITDA = Total Financed Debt / EBITDA

blocks.text: Ability to manage its debt load relative to its earnings potential. Lower FDER indicates that the company's funded debt is relatively lower compared to its earnings.

title: Customer economics: churn, acquisition, retention and recurring revenue
summary: Connect customer measures with acquisition cost, recurring-revenue movements and unit economics.
takeaway: Match cohorts, periods and revenue-versus-profit definitions before interpreting a customer metric.
steps: Churn, buyer growth, lifetime value and acquisition cost
Revenue per customer and SaaS quick ratio
Contract value, movements and budget labels
notes: The source’s net-dollar-retention numerator is unspecified; the reviewed expression tracks the opening cohort and excludes new-customer revenue. SaaS quick ratio uses new MRR, not total or net ending MRR.

The expansion/contraction formulas cannot isolate individual movements from aggregate period totals. The reviewed movement definitions require customer-level recurring-revenue data. “Budget attainment” is not the same as variance divided by budget.
Revenue LTV is not contribution/profit LTV. Customer acquisition and payback need compatible cost allocation, customer counts and gross-profit periods.

references.title: Stripe: monthly and annual recurring revenue

sections.heading: Churn, buyer growth, lifetime value and acquisition cost

formula.name: Customer churn rate
formula.expression: Opening-cohort customers lost during period / customers at period start
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Customers lost: opening-cohort customers meeting the churn definition.
Opening customers: eligible starting customer base.
formula.scope: The source says total customers without specifying timing. New customers should not silently dilute an opening-cohort loss rate.
original: Customer Churn Rate = Customers lost / Total Customers
Percentage of customers lost in a given time frame

references.title: Stripe: monthly and annual recurring revenue

formula.name: New-buyer growth
formula.expression: (New buyers this period − new buyers prior period) / new buyers prior period
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: New buyers: distinct buyers meeting the acquisition definition in each comparable period.
formula.scope: Not total-customer growth; prior-period zero makes the rate undefined.
original: New Buyer Growth Rate = (New buyers this month - New buyers last month) / New buyers last month
Speed at which you gain new customers over defined periods of time

formula.name: Simple revenue lifetime value
formula.expression: Revenue per customer per period × expected customer lifespan in periods
inputs: Period revenue: compatible expected revenue per customer.
Lifespan: expected duration in the same periods.
formula.scope: A constant-average revenue approximation, not profit/contribution LTV, discounted cash value or a guaranteed lifetime.
original: Lifetime Value = Customer Value x Average Customer Lifespan
Revenue from a customer over the retention time period

formula.name: Customer acquisition cost
formula.expression: Attributed sales and marketing cost / matching new customers acquired
inputs: Attributed costs: declared acquisition cost allocation.
New customers: acquisition cohort matching those costs.
formula.scope: Allow for sales-cycle timing and attribution. Revenue growth and customer acquisition are different outcomes.
original: Customer Acquisition Costs = Cost of Sales and Marketing / Number of New Customers Acquired
Amount of money a company spends to get a new customer

sections.heading: Revenue per customer and SaaS quick ratio

formula.name: Revenue per customer
formula.expression: Period revenue / stated matching customer base
inputs: Revenue: defined customer revenue.
Customer base: declared average/active/point-in-time count.
formula.scope: Customer and user counts differ. State period and population; a closing count is not automatically comparable to an average.
original: Average Revenue per User = Total Revenue / Total number of customers
Average revenue generated per customer (either monthy or annually)

references.title: Stripe: monthly and annual recurring revenue

formula.name: SaaS quick ratio
formula.expression: (New MRR + expansion MRR) / (churned MRR + contraction MRR)
inputs: New/expansion MRR: additions in normalized monthly recurring value.
Churn/contraction MRR: positive magnitudes of lost recurring value.
formula.scope: The source’s “net MRR” is ambiguous; the displayed convention uses new MRR. Define reactivation policy and avoid confusing this with the financial quick ratio.
original: SaaS Quick Ratio = (Net Monthly Recurring Revenue period [MRRt] + Expansion MRRt) / (Churned MRRt + Contraction MRRt)
Compares revenue added (new business) vs. revenue lost (churn)

references.title: Stripe: monthly and annual recurring revenue

formula.name: Uniform-customer MRR shortcut
formula.expression: Eligible customers × average normalized monthly recurring amount
inputs: Customers: eligible active subscriptions/customers.
Monthly amount: recurring charge normalized to a month.
formula.scope: Exclude nonrecurring items and define subscription states; annual billing is not all MRR in the payment month.
original: Monthly Recurring Revenue = Number of customers x Average billed amount
Monthly revenue from customers with a subscription

references.title: Stripe: monthly and annual recurring revenue

formula.name: Net revenue retention for an opening cohort
formula.expression: (Opening-cohort MRR + expansion − contraction − churn) / opening-cohort MRR × 100
inputs: Opening-cohort MRR: recurring value of customers present at start.
Movements: only changes for that cohort, with loss amounts positive.
formula.scope: Exclude new-customer revenue. The source’s “net revenue” does not supply this cohort definition; state reactivation policy.
original: Net Dollar Retention = Net Revenue / Opening MRR
The amount being retained from a customer or cohort over a specific period of time

references.title: Stripe: monthly and annual recurring revenue

formula.name: Gross-profit CAC payback
formula.expression: CAC per acquired customer / gross profit per customer per period
inputs: CAC: acquisition cost per new customer.
Gross profit: expected revenue less corresponding cost of sales per customer and period.
formula.scope: The source omits per-customer/per-period matching. A zero/negative gross profit does not provide a positive payback time.
original: CAC Paybank = Customer Acquisition Cost / Gross Profit
Period of time till you make back your CAC

sections.heading: Contract value, movements and budget labels

formula.name: Average annual contract value
formula.expression: Total annualized eligible contract value / eligible contract count
inputs: Annualized value: recurring/eligible contract value normalized to a year.
Contract count: matching eligible contracts.
formula.scope: The source uses total revenue without annualization. Contract value, recognized revenue and one-time fees need separate treatment.
original: Average Contract Value = Total Revenue / No. of Contracts
The average contract value from a customer (more common in B2B)

references.title: Stripe: monthly and annual recurring revenue

formula.name: Expansion recurring revenue
formula.expression: Sum of positive recurring-value increases for continuing customers
inputs: Expansion movements: customer-level upgrades/additions under a stated policy.
formula.scope: Aggregate period revenue minus reactivation/churn cannot isolate expansion. Define cohort and exclude new/reactivated customer value as appropriate.
original: Expansion Revenue = (Total Revenue in Current Period - Total Revenue in Previous Period) - (Reactivation Revenue + Churn Revenue)
Added revenue from recurring customers

references.title: Stripe: monthly and annual recurring revenue

formula.name: Contraction recurring revenue
formula.expression: Sum of partial recurring-value reductions for continuing customers
inputs: Contraction movements: positive magnitudes of downgrades/reductions.
formula.scope: Separate partial downgrades from full churn; aggregate revenue totals cannot isolate contraction reliably.
original: Contraction revenue = (Total Revenue in Previous Period - Total Revenue in Current Period) + Downgrade Revenue + Churn Revenue
Reduced revenue from recurring customers

references.title: Stripe: monthly and annual recurring revenue

formula.name: Budget attainment versus variance
formula.expression: Attainment = actual / budget; variance rate = (actual − budget) / budget
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Actual/budget: same measure, period, units and perimeter.
formula.scope: The source labels variance/budget as attainment. Favorable/unfavorable signs depend on whether the measure is cost, revenue or another target.
original: Budget Attainment = Budget variance / Budget Amount
% of your budget achieved

formula.name: Revenue per user
formula.expression: Period revenue / stated matching user base
inputs: Revenue: defined relevant revenue.
Users: eligible user count, with average/active/closing timing declared.
formula.scope: Users, paying accounts and customers are different populations; do not silently interchange ARPU/ARPA definitions.
original: Average Revenue per User = Total Revenue / No. of User
The average revenue you are generating from a user (more common in B2C)

title: Cash-flow statements: operations, investment and financing
summary: Separate profit from cash movements and classify the flows behind the cash balance.
takeaway: Reconcile the beginning and ending cash balance and explain every material movement.
steps: Cash balance and the indirect operating bridge
notes: The source’s direct/indirect descriptions are study shorthand. Interest/dividend and other classifications depend on the applicable framework and reporting period; do not apply one universal list without checking it. Cash balance reconciliations may also require exchange-rate and other reconciling effects.

sections.heading: Cash balance and the indirect operating bridge

formula.name: Cash-balance reconciliation
formula.expression: Closing cash = opening cash + operating + investing + financing cash flows + applicable reconciling effects
inputs: Opening/closing cash: balances on a consistent cash definition.
Activity cash flows: signed inflows less outflows.
Reconciling effects: applicable exchange-rate and other reconciliation items.
formula.scope: The source’s three-flow bridge is simplified; include material required reconciling effects.
original: Ending cash = Beginning Cash + Cash from Operating Activities + Cash from Investing Activities + Cash from Finance Activities

items: Inflow or outflow resulting from a company's day-to-day operating activities.Fixed asset and long term assets.Debt / equity raised / paid.

blocks.text: Presented through direct or indirect method.Direct method easier to understand and difficult to produce.Indirect method easier to produce and challenging to understand.

formula.name: Indirect operating-cash-flow bridge
formula.expression: Net income + signed noncash adjustments − increase in noncash operating working capital + other required operating reconciliations
inputs: Signed noncash adjustments: add noncash charges and remove applicable gains/items.
Increase in operating working capital: investment in noncash operating balances.
formula.scope: Framework and interest/tax classifications matter. CAPEX is cash capital expenditure expressed as a positive outflow; ΔNWC is an increase in noncash operating working capital, excluding financing debt. Reconcile classification and other noncash/operating adjustments.
original: Operating Cash Flow (OCF) = Net Income + Depreciation + Amortisation + Other Non-Cash Items - Changes in Working Capital

A measure of a company's cash inflow and outflow from its primary business activities. A higher OCF indicates that a company has more cash available for its day-to-day operations, investments, and debt repayments.

formula.name: Net activity cash flow
formula.expression: Operating + investing + financing cash flows
inputs: Each activity flow: signed cash inflows less cash outflows in that class.
formula.scope: This is the net of activity flows; the total cash reconciliation can also include FX and other required effects.
original: Net Cash Flow = Operating Cash Flow + Investing Cash Flow + Financing Cash Flow
The total amount of cash generated or used by a company from its operating, investing, and financing activities. Positive cash flow indicates that a company is generating more cash than it is using.

blocks.text: Inflows

items: Cash received from collections of accounts receivable
Cash received as interest and dividends

blocks.text: Outflows

items: Cash paid to suppliers and employee
Cash interest payments made on debt

blocks.text: Investing cash flow
Inflows

items: Cash received from the sales of property, plant, and equipment
Cash received from the sales of investments
Cash received from repayments of loans made to others

blocks.text: Outflows

items: Cash paid for the purchase of property, plant, and equipment
Cash paid for the purchase of investments
Cash paid out to others as loans

blocks.text: Financing cash flow
Inflows

items: Cash received from issuing new common or preferred stock
Cash received from the issuance of bonds or bank borrowings
Cash received from the sale of treasury stock

blocks.text: Outflows

items: Cash paid to repurchase common or preferred stock
Cash paid to repay debt principal
Cash paid out to shareholders as dividends

title: Free cash flow: distinguish operating, firm and equity cash
summary: Reconcile reinvestment, working capital, interest and net borrowing before choosing a free-cash-flow measure.
takeaway: Match the cash-flow definition to its recipients and discount rate.
steps: A common operating-cash-flow less CAPEX measure
Operating, investing, financing and stakeholder bridges
Correcting the source’s fixed-asset and equity-cash expressions
notes: Several source expressions confuse balances with changes and omit reinvestment or financing movements. The reviewed bridges use explicit positive CAPEX, increases in non-cash working capital and net borrowing conventions.
An OCF-based FCFF bridge assumes interest is included in operating cash flow and tax treatment is compatible; otherwise use the EBIT-based bridge and reconcile classifications.

sections.heading: A common operating-cash-flow less CAPEX measure

formula.name: Operating cash flow less capital expenditure
formula.expression: Operating cash flow − cash CAPEX
inputs: OCF: reported operating cash flow on the declared basis.
Cash CAPEX: cash investment in long-lived operating assets.
formula.scope: A common non-GAAP FCF convention; distinguish it from FCFF/FCFE and define included investment.
original: Free Cash Flow (FCF) = Operating Cash Flow - Capital Expenditures

Free cash flow measures a company's cash flow available for distribution to its investors or for future investments. A positive FCF indicates that a company is generating cash from its operations and co-invest in new projects, pay dividents, or reduce debt.

formula.name: Free cash flow to the firm: operating-profit bridge
formula.expression: EBIT × (1 − tax rate) + noncash operating charges − CAPEX − increase in noncash operating working capital
inputs: EBIT: compatible operating earnings basis.
Tax rate: operating-tax assumption.
Noncash charges: eligible noncash operating expenses.
formula.scope: The tax/operating basis must be suitable for the model. CAPEX is cash capital expenditure expressed as a positive outflow; ΔNWC is an increase in noncash operating working capital, excluding financing debt. Reconcile classification and other noncash/operating adjustments.
original: Unlevered Free Cash Flow = EBIT (1 - Tax Rate) + Depreciation & Amortization - Capital Expenditures - Changes in Working Capital

It represents the cash generated by a company's core operations that is available to all investors, regardless of its capital structure. A higher UFCF indicates that the company is generating more cash from its core operations.

formula.name: Free cash flow to equity: full earnings bridge
formula.expression: Net income + noncash charges − CAPEX − increase in noncash operating working capital + net borrowing
inputs: Net income: earnings after interest and tax.
Net borrowing: new debt proceeds less principal repayments.
Noncash charges: required earnings-to-cash adjustments.
formula.scope: The source’s EBITDA-minus-tax/CAPEX/interest shortcut omits working-capital and net-borrowing effects. CAPEX is cash capital expenditure expressed as a positive outflow; ΔNWC is an increase in noncash operating working capital, excluding financing debt. Reconcile classification and other noncash/operating adjustments.
original: Levered Free Cash Flow = EBITDA - Taxes - Capital Expenditures - Interest Expense

The cash flow available to equity shareholders after deducting interest payments on debt and incorporating any net borrowings. Higher LFCF indicates that the company has strong cash flow available to its equity shareholders even after servicing its debt.

sections.heading: Operating, investing, financing and stakeholder bridges

formula.name: Operating cash flow: reconcile working-capital signs
formula.expression: Net income + signed noncash adjustments − increase in noncash operating working capital + required operating reconciliations
inputs: Noncash adjustments: signed earnings-to-cash adjustments.
Working-capital increase: positive investment in noncash operating balances.
formula.scope: The source adds “changes” without defining their sign. Define investment increases versus signed cash effects explicitly. CAPEX is cash capital expenditure expressed as a positive outflow; ΔNWC is an increase in noncash operating working capital, excluding financing debt. Reconcile classification and other noncash/operating adjustments.
original: Operating Cash Flow = Net Income + Depreciation and Amortisation + Non-cash Items + Changes in Net Working Capital

formula.name: Investing cash flow
formula.expression: Cash investing receipts − cash investing payments
inputs: Investing receipts/payments: relevant disposals, acquisitions, lending and investment cash flows.
formula.scope: Net CAPEX is only part of investing cash flow, with a stated sign; the source equates them too broadly.
original: Investing Cash Flow = Net Capital Expenditures (CAPEX)

formula.name: Financing cash flow
formula.expression: Debt proceeds − principal repayments + equity proceeds − share repurchases − distributions + other financing flows
inputs: Debt/equity movements: relevant cash financing receipts and payments.
formula.scope: The source’s “net debt process” appears to mean proceeds. Define distributions, lease/debt repayments and framework-dependent classification.
original: Financing Cash Flow = Net Debt Process + Net Equity Proceeds

formula.name: FCFF: operating-cash-flow bridge
formula.expression: Operating cash flow − cash CAPEX + compatible after-tax interest adjustment
inputs: OCF: operating cash flow after the interest deduction being adjusted.
After-tax interest: compatible interest × (1 − tax rate).
formula.scope: Valid only with compatible interest and tax classifications; otherwise use/reconcile an operating-profit bridge.
original: Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF) or Unlevered CF = Operating CF - CAPEX + Interest Expense x (1-tax)

formula.name: FCFE: operating-cash-flow bridge
formula.expression: Operating cash flow − cash CAPEX + net borrowing
inputs: OCF: compatible after-interest/tax operating cash flow.
Net borrowing: debt proceeds less principal repayment.
formula.scope: Reconcile cash-flow classifications and other required equity-cash adjustments. CAPEX is cash capital expenditure expressed as a positive outflow; ΔNWC is an increase in noncash operating working capital, excluding financing debt. Reconcile classification and other noncash/operating adjustments.
original: Free Cash Flow to Equity (FCFE) or Levered CF = Operating CF - CAPEX + Net Debt Proceeds

sections.heading: Correcting the source’s fixed-asset and equity-cash expressions

formula.name: FCFF: correct the fixed-asset shorthand
formula.expression: Operating cash flow + compatible after-tax interest − cash CAPEX
inputs: OCF/interest: compatible classifications.
Cash CAPEX: actual relevant cash investment, not an unexplained change in asset balance.
formula.scope: Changes in fixed assets can include depreciation, disposals and noncash movements; they are not automatically CAPEX.
original: Free Cash Flow to the Firm = Operating Cash Flow + Interest x (1 - Tax Rate) + Changes in Fixed Assets

items: Cash generated by a company's core operations available to all stakeholders.

formula.name: FCFE: use changes, not balance totals
formula.expression: Net income + noncash charges − cash CAPEX − increase in noncash operating working capital + net borrowing
inputs: Working-capital changes: relevant noncash operating balance changes, not sums of their balances.
Net borrowing: new debt less principal repaid.
formula.scope: The source adds receivable, payable, inventory and other balances and CAPEX without a defined reconciliation. CAPEX is cash capital expenditure expressed as a positive outflow; ΔNWC is an increase in noncash operating working capital, excluding financing debt. Reconcile classification and other noncash/operating adjustments.
original: Free Cash Flow to Equity = Net Income + Depreciation and Amortisation + Accounts Receivables + Accounts Payable + Inventory Balances + Current Assets and Liabilities + CAPEX + Net Borrowing

items: Cash available to a company's equity shareholders after all expenses, capital expenditures, and debt payments.

title: Working-capital cycle: DSO, DPO and inventory days
summary: Follow the operating cash cycle and examine collection, payment and inventory choices.
takeaway: Measure the cash cycle consistently and balance liquidity with supplier and customer relationships.
steps: Overdues, repeated inventory days and the mislabeled DSO
notes: The second “DSO” expression uses payables and describes supplier settlement; it is a payable-days variant, not sales collection. Purchases and cost of sales are not interchangeable unless the proxy is disclosed.

Use the actual period length; multiplying a quarterly ratio by 365 is not automatically appropriate. Longer supplier payment is not automatically beneficial if it creates fees, loss of discounts or supply problems.

references.title: ACCA: performance appraisal and working-capital ratios

formula.name: Cash conversion cycle
formula.expression: Inventory days + receivable days − payable days
inputs: Inventory days: stock holding duration.
Receivable days: customer collection duration.
Payable days: supplier payment duration.
formula.scope: Use matching periods and compatible balance/flow definitions. A negative cycle can occur in some business models.
original: Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) = Days of Inventory Outstanding + Days of Sales Outstanding - Days of Payables Outstanding
The time to converts its inventory and receivables minus the time to pay its supplier. Low CCC means efficient management and has cash available to pay obligations and invest in growth opportunities.

references.title: ACCA: performance appraisal and working-capital ratios

formula.name: Receivable days (DSO)
formula.expression: Average trade receivables / net credit sales × period days
inputs: Average receivables: compatible customer balance.
Credit sales: sales creating those receivables.
Period days: actual days for the sales period.
formula.scope: The source abbreviates one entry as DSP; the intended collection-duration measure is DSO.
original: Day Sales Outstanding (DSP) = Average Accounts Receivables / Net Credit Sales x 365
How long, on average, it takes for a company to collect payments from its customers for credit sales. A lower DSO indicates that the company is collecting its receivables more quickly.

references.title: ACCA: performance appraisal and working-capital ratios

formula.name: Payable days (DPO)
formula.expression: Average trade payables / credit purchases × period days
inputs: Average payables: matching supplier balance.
Credit purchases: purchases creating those obligations.
Period days: days covered by purchases.

formula.name: Discounted cash-flow sum
formula.expression: Σ CFₜ / (1 + r)ᵗ
inputs: CFₜ: cash flow at the end of period t.
r: compatible discount rate per period.
t: time periods from the valuation date.

original: Discounted Cash Flow = CF1 / (1 + r)^1 + CF2 / (1 + r)^2 + ... + CFn / (1 + r)^n
Valuing an investment or a company by discounting its expected future cash flows to their present value. High DCF indicates the company is expected to generate more cash in the future.

formula.name: Present value of a single cash flow
formula.expression: CF / (1 + r)ⁿ
inputs: CF: future cash amount.
r: discount rate per period.
n: number of matching periods.
formula.scope: Assumes a specified cash-flow timing and rate; noninteger/irregular timing requires an appropriate convention.

It measures the current value of a future cash flo, given a discount rate. A higher PV indicates that the future cash flow is more valuable today.

formula.name: Future value of a single amount
formula.expression: PV × (1 + r)ⁿ
inputs: PV: starting amount.
r: compound return/interest rate per period.
n: matching compounding periods.
formula.scope: Assumes a constant rate and stated compounding convention; not a guaranteed investment return.

inputs: Initial investment: initial positive outlay.

inputs: Next-period cash flow: first flow after the explicit forecast.

sections.heading: The valuation workflow and the source’s cost-of-equity expression

blocks.text: DCF is used to estimate the intrinsic value of an investment or business by discounting future cash flows to their present value. It helps determine whether an investment opportunity is undervalued or overvalued.
DCF Usage

The discount rate is the minimum rate of return acceptable to the investor. The absolute value of the discount rate depends on the definition of the discount rate. Namely, for cash flow after debt servicing, a simple discount rate is used, while for cash flow before debt servicing, a weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is used.
Forecasting capital expenditures (capex) is an important part of the valuation modelling process, as it allows businesses to plan for and manage their investment in long-term assets.

The cost of equity is the expected rate of return that shareholders require to invest in a company’s common equity. In other words, it is the return that investors expect to receive on their investment in the form of dividends and capital gains. When conducting a valuation, the cost of equity is an important factor to consider as it reflects the investors' perception of risk associated with the company's future earnings. A higher risk perception means a higher cost of equity, and vice versa.

formula.name: CAPM cost of equity
formula.expression: Risk-free rate + equity beta × (expected market return − risk-free rate)
inputs: Risk-free rate: compatible currency/horizon assumption.
Equity beta: equity-risk estimate.
Expected market return: market return assumption.
formula.scope: This is a cost-of-equity model, not a universal discount rate. FCFF and FCFE require matched discount rates and cash definitions.
original: Discount Rate = risk free rate + investment beta (market rate - risk free rate)

Compare EBIT to Revenue: What is the percentage or EBIT to your revenue? Is this percentage increasing or decreasing over time?
Compare EBIT to COGS: How does EBIT compare to the cost of goods sold (COGS)? Is the ratio increasing or decreasing?
EBIT Margin; Calculate your EBIT margin (EBIT divided by revenue)- How does this figure compare to industry benchmarks?
Year-on-year EBIT: Compare your EBIT on a year-on~year basis. Is it growing staying steady. or decreasing?
EBIT per Employee? How much EBIT does each employee generate? Is this figure increasing or decreasing?
EBIT by Product Line: Calculate EBIT for each product or service line. Which are the most and least profitable?
EBIT by Business Unit: Does your business have multiple units or departments, calculate the EBIT for each Which units are driving profitability?
Forecasting EBIT: Forecast EBIT for the next quarter. year, and three years. How do these projections compare to your strategic goals?
EBIT Sensitivity Analysis: Conduct a sensitivity analysis tor am. How do changes in sales volume, price. or costs affect EBIT?
Compare EBIT to Operating Cash Flow: How does EBIT compare to operating cash flow? Significant differences might indicate issues with working capital management.
EBIT and Capital Expendim: How does EBIT compare to your capital expenditure? High capital expenditure with low EBIT may indicate a need for efficiency improvements.
EBIT and Interest Expense: If you have significant debt, compare EBIT to your interest expense. Can your operational earnings cover interest payments?
EBIT and taxation: How does EBIT compareto your tax expense? This can provide insight into your effective tax rate.
EBIT and Dividends: Can your EBIT cover your dividend payments? If not, you might need to reevaluate your dividend policy.
EBIT and Investment: Compare EBIT to your investment income. This can show you how much of your profitability is driven by operations versus investments.
EBIT and Non-Operating Expenses: How does EBIT compare to hon-oparoting expenses? High non-operating expenses can distort your operational profitability.
EBIT and Depreciation: How does EBIT compare to depreciation? This can indicate whether your assets are generating sufficient profits.
EBIT and Amortisation If you have significant intangible assets, compare EBIT to amortisation this can help access the profitability at those assets.

sections.heading: Strengths and weaknesses in the source

blocks.text: Strength

items: Relatively easy to calculate using information from a company's income statement and can be a simplified way to evaluate financial performance.

It can be a useful metric for comparing the performance of companies across industries and geographies, as it removes the impact of different tax rates, capital financing and capital structures in the comparison.
It can be used to evaluate a company's ability to generate cash flow from its operations, but only for companies with low CAPEX and slow growth.
It helps to identify trends in a company's operating performance over time, assuming a consistent formula is used across periods.
It helps exclude the impact of financing, capital investments and tax planning decisions from a company's operating performance.
It is often used as a valuation metric in mergers and acquisitions and can be useful as a benchmark for determining the value of a company.

blocks.text: Weakness

items: Not a standardised GAAP metric which allows for wide variation in how it is calculated.
Its use cases often imply that all income converts equally to cash, which is not accurate in practice.
Does not consider the required capital reinvestment.
Does not consider cash absorbed into working capital assets.
Could imply loan repayments will be made in priority which may not happen.
Doesn't reflect the quality of earnings which can lead to potential overstatement.
Poor measure of profitability due to differing accounting standards around the world.
Can't really compare acquisition multiples as it lacks industry specifics.
Can be misleading as it ignores real cash outflows like interest and taxes.

title: Accounts payable controls: responsibilities, checks and risks
summary: Compare payment, vendor, coding, matching and reconciliation controls in a structured matrix.
takeaway: Clear responsibility and independent review help reduce risk but do not guarantee fraud prevention.
notes: The matrix is a design reference, not evidence of operating effectiveness. Small teams may need compensating controls; system access, exception handling and review quality matter.

blocks.text: Control Overview

rows: Segregation of Duties (SOD) is a fundamental internal control principle that involves dividing key tasks and responsibilities among multiple individuals or departments.
Authorization - The approval or permission to perform a transaction. Recording— The documentation and recording of transactions. Custody- The physical control or handling of assets.
SOD ensures that no single individual has end-to-end control over a critical financial process, minimizing the potential for misuse or errors.

The Preparer-Checker Control is an internal control designed to enhance accuracy and reliability in financial processes. The two individuals involved in a transaction are the "preparer" and the "checker."
The preparer initiates the transaction or prepares the documentation while the Checker independently reviews and verifies the accuracy of the work performed by the preparer.
This control is particularly effective in mitigating errors, preventing fraud, and ensuring that financial transactions meet the organization's standards.

Establish a clear hierarchy for authorizing payments. Different individuals should be responsible for approving invoices and authorizing payments, with higher amounts requiring additional levels of approval.
Authorization— The person approving the payment should not have access to recording invoices. Recording— The person recording invoices and payments should not be authorized to approve payments.
Mitigating the risk of one individual being able to record and release payments without any checks and balances.
Vendor verification and approval are integral components of the accounts payable process, ensuring that organizations engage with legitimate and reputable suppliers.
The preparer initiates the vendor onboarding process, ensuring that all submitted vendor information is verified for accuracy and legitimacy. The approver independently reviews the vendor information
This control mechanism involves a systematic approach to validating vendors' identity, authenticity, and reliability before establishing business relationships or processing transactions.
Matching invoices with corresponding purchase orders and receiving reports (three-way match) is a critical step to ensure that the organization is billed accurately for goods or services received.
Match Purchase Order, Goods Receipt Note and invoice to ensure the accuracy of goods and services, quantity, unit and total price match across all three documents.
Three-way matching ensures accurate billing and prevents unauthorized or duplicate payments.
Accurate Coding and Classification of Expenses
This control ensures that each transaction is correctly identified, categorized, and recorded in the organization's accounting system.
The preparer codes and classifies expenses. The checker/approver reviews the coding as part of the approval process.
Implement controls to ensure that invoices are accurately coded and classified according to proper GL accounts, cost centers, or projects, facilitating accurate financial reporting and analysis.

Invoice and payment reconciliation are critical internal controls. It involves comparing and verifying invoices with corresponding payments to ensure accuracy, completeness, and adherence to financial policies.
AP staff is often responsible for initiating the reconciliation process. A supervisor reviews the reconciliation conducted by the AP staff member. This adds an additional layer of verification.
Reconciliation ensures that the amounts on invoices match the actual payments made. This accuracy is fundamental for reliable financial reporting. It also helps prevent fraud and errors.

Duplicate payments occur when the same invoice is paid more than once, leading to financial discrepancies. A Duplicate Payment Prevention control is essential for maintaining financial accuracy and preventing fraud.
Implement controls within the accounting system that can detect and flag potential duplicates as invoices are entered into the system, preventing erroneous payments before they occur.
Preventing duplicate payments ensures that financial records accurately reflect the accurate liabilities and expenses. It helps avoid payments otherwise being erroneously disbursed.
AP Sub-Ledger and General Ledger Reconciliation
The reconciliation between the Accounts Payable (AP) sub-ledger and the General Ledger is a critical internal control mechanism that ensures accuracy and consistency in financial reporting.
Conduct regular reconciliations between the AP sub-Ledger and the General Ledger. It should be done at least monthly. This includes verifying that the amounts, accounts, and transaction dates align.

By reconciling the AP sub-Ledger with the General Ledger, the organization can identify and correct any data entry errors, ensuring the accuracy and integrity issues between the sub-ledger and the general ledger.

formula.name: Transfer-pricing operating net margin
formula.expression: Relevant operating net profit / relevant sales
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Operating net profit: result on the tested transaction/entity scope.

formula.scope: A profit-level indicator is not an automatic arm’s-length result; comparability and tested-party selection matter.

formula.name: Net cost-plus / return on total costs
formula.expression: Relevant operating net profit / relevant operating cost base
formula.units: ratio; multiply by 100 to express a percentage
inputs: Profit: tested operating result.
Cost base: defined costs relevant to the tested activity.
formula.scope: Pass-through costs and accounting classifications affect comparability. Do not assume every company expense belongs in the denominator.

formula.expression: Relevant gross profit / relevant operating expenses
inputs: Gross profit: tested gross return.
Operating expenses: appropriate operating cost base.

blocks.text: Compares the price charged in a controlled transaction to the price charged in a comparable uncontrolled transaction. Useful for commodity transactions. financial transactions. and transactions with very reliable internal comparables

Assesses the gross margin with which a product purchased in the controlled transaction was resold in the uncontrolled transaction. Most appropriate for sales. marketing. and distribution transactions where internal compomics are available.

Test the gross markup on costs incurred by an enterprise during transactions with related parties. Suitable for manufacturing and service provision transactions where internal comparables are available.

Tests the net (operating) profit earned by a tested party of a controlled transaction. Often applied when a tested party can be identified no internal comparables are available and traditional methods are not reliable. TNMM is versatile and flexible and typically relies on external comparabies.

Splits the profits to arrive at the result that would be achieved by independent parties in comparable transactions. Used for transactions where both parties make unique and valuable contributions (such as intangibles), and/or traditional methods are not appropriate due to the high integration of business operations.
Adjustments in transfer pricing
Changes that make the characteristics of uncontrolled transactions more comparable, enabling their use in transfer pricing method applications.
Changes that taxpayers can make at year-end to bring the results of their transactions Into the arm’s length range.
Adjustments to a company's taxable profits made by a tax administration due to the application of the arm's length principle.These adjustments may lead to double taxation issues.
Changes to the tax liability of a related party mode by the second tax jurisdiction corresponding to a primary adjustment. These adjustments are intended to resolve double taxation.

Constructive transactions introduced after a primary adjustment to align actual profit allocation with the primary adjustment. Can take the form of constructive dividends, equity contributions, or loans.
